answer.answer:
To design for manufacture and assembly with robots, put the design conditions in place first: standardise the components, keep the architecture modular, bring the contractor into early design and build the parametric toolchain, because only one of those four requirements is a tool and the other three are properties of the design and the organisation. DfMA then pushes the work off site, and this matters because robotic assembly takes prefabrication as its precondition: the robots attach to the prefabricated components, not to the design method itself, so there is no direct route from DfMA to a robot without passing through off-site production. Standardisation is the strongest single lever, carrying both the DfMA link and the robotic assembly link. The material in front of me is literature-derived and coded-case counts only, with no deployed project or company record for this question, so nothing here rests on a named deployment.

**What DfMA for DFAB requires (the complete set of edges)**

PR9 "DfMA for DFAB process" is a Process that applies in the Design phase, spans Design to Structural Construction, and plays a design-for-X role [1]. It carries 3 inbound and 3 outbound dependency edges, and 15 of the 50 coded cases draw on it. [2] Read by relation rather than by arrow direction, four things sit upstream of it:

- AT7 "Highly standardised" (Attribute), which enables PR9 on peer-reviewed evidence, an edge carried by 13 of the 50 coded cases [2]; 25 of the 50 cases draw on AT7 [2]. Design standardisation and simplification is the DfMA enabler here. [3]
- CO11 "Early contractor involvement" (Condition), enabling PR9 on peer-reviewed evidence, carried by 11 of the 50 cases, on the grounds that early collaboration is among the DfMA enablers for offsite work [2]; 14 of the 50 cases draw on CO11 [2].
- RE1 "Parametric/computational/data-driven algorithm/machine code" (Resource), the one requirement that is a tool: PR9 dependsOn RE1 on peer-reviewed evidence, carried by 8 of the 50 cases, because the DfMA-oriented process combines DfMA with BIM parametric design to support manufacture and assembly [2]; 11 of the 50 cases draw on RE1 [2].
- AT2 "Modular" (Attribute), enabling PR9 on peer-reviewed evidence, carried by 7 of the 50 cases, through alignment of product modularity and process modularity [2]; 12 of the 50 cases draw on AT2 [2].

Standardisation and modularity reinforce each other in both directions: AT7 enables AT2, carried by 11 cases [2], and AT2 enables AT7, also carried by 11 cases [2]. Bespoke work pulls against this: AT1 "Bespoke/customised design" constrains AT2, an edge carried by 4 of the 50 cases [2].

**What DfMA delivers**

PR9 enables PR2 "Prefabrication/off-site", on the grounds that DfMA orients the project toward offsite manufacture [4], an edge carried by 15 of the 50 cases [2], and PR9 enables PR5 "Modularisation", carried by 8 of the 50 cases [2]. Those two are its complete downstream set. Prefabrication in turn carries the value: reduced time and improved productivity, carried by 19 cases [2], improved quality, carried by 18 [2], fewer errors and reworks, carried by 14 [2], and improved site safety, carried by 12 [2]. It also imports two exposures: PR2 dependsOn RI14 "Rely on precise planning", carried by 18 cases [2], and PR2 dependsOn RI18 "Regulatory/legal concern", carried by 10 cases, because offsite compliance requires third-party certification and traceability [2].

**Where the robots attach**

None of PR9's six edges touches a robotic enabler, so the connection is indirect and runs through prefabrication: PR4 "Robotic assembly" hasPrecondition PR2 "Prefabrication/off-site", an edge carried by 4 of the 50 cases, on the finding that automated overhead delivery and assembly requires extensive prefabrication and unification of materials [2]. 13 of the 50 cases draw on PR4. [2] Its other requirements are RE2 "Robotic arm", carried by 12 of the 50 cases [2] (22 of 50 cases draw on RE2 [2]), PR12 "Path-planning", which enables PR4 on an edge carried by only 2 of the 50 cases [2], and AT7 "Highly standardised", which enables PR4 on an edge carried by 10 of the 50 cases, Japanese automated erection systems being reliant on standardised prefabricated components [2]. That second AT7 edge is why standardisation is the strongest lever here: it is the one enabler that pays into both the DfMA process and the robotic assembly step. Note also that CO12 "Mobile factory" (a Condition) is cited in the literature as enabling PR4 but is carried by none of the 50 coded cases [2], and only 1 of the 50 cases draws on CO12 at all [2].

On outcomes, robotic assembly amplifies rather than transforms: PR4 amplifies VA2 "Reduce time/improve productivity/efficiency", carried by 13 cases [2], amplifies VA6 "Reduce cost", carried by 7 [2], and enables VA10 "Reduce errors/constraints" on an edge carried by just 1 of the 50 cases [2], the error-reduction claim therefore being much better supported through prefabrication than through the robot. One organisational exposure sits under it: PR4 dependsOn RI12 "Delivery/business model/work culture", carried by 2 cases, robotics adoption in precast production resting on the environmental and organisational context [2].

**Operating the cell**

32 of the 50 coded cases draw on CO6 "Human-robot interaction" [2], and its requirements are blunt: CO6 dependsOn RI6 "Require workforce training", an edge carried by 27 of the 50 cases and the most heavily carried edge in this material [2], with 44 of the 50 cases drawing on RI6 [2]. CO6 also dependsOn RI18 "Regulatory/legal concern" on standards evidence, carried by 2 cases, compliance with robot safety standards being the requirement [2], and CO6 mitigates RI20 "Work safety concern" on standards evidence, carried by 4 cases, through power-and-force-limiting collaborative operation within biomechanical limits [2]. Budget for training before hardware.

**Limits of this evidence**

Retrieval widened "robotics" to include gantry systems and mobile robots; that changes little, since RE10 "Gantry-type robotic system" is drawn on by 5 of the 50 cases and carries no dependency edges at all [2], and no mobile-vehicle enabler appears in the material in front of me. No Process RP record or CensusProcess record and no firm appears here, so this is a design-of-dependencies answer, not a report of a deployed line. The edge counts above are exact and complete for PR9, PR4 and the other enablers listed in the dependency section; the co-occurrence figures are statistical association only, and the 2797 co-occurrence edges touching these enablers were cut to the 15 strongest [2], so nothing about the absence of a relation can be read from them.
